claim: Human IRE1α is a 977 amino-acid protein composed of an N-terminal ER-lumenal domain (LD), a single-pass transmembrane (TM) domain, and a C-terminal cytoplasmic domain (CD).
source: Human IRE1α (herein IRE1) is a 977 amino-acid protein (Figure 1A), composed of an N-terminal ER-lumenal domain (LD), a single-pass transmembrane (TM) domain, and a C-terminal cytoplasmic domain (CD).
evidence: This is a structural description of IRE1 protein based on established knowledge of its domain organization.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of IRE1 consists of a membrane-proximal 'linker' region, followed by a serine/threonine kinase domain, and an endoribonuclease (RNase) moiety.
source: The CD segment consists of three parts: a membrane-proximal 'linker' region, followed by a serine/threonine kinase domain, and an endoribonuclease (RNase) moiety.
evidence: This describes the structural organization of IRE1's cytoplasmic domain based on established knowledge.

claim: ER stress leads to caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1 in KMS11 and OPM2 multiple myeloma cell lines.
source: WB analysis with the anti-IRE1 LD antibody revealed not only the presence of the full-length ~105 kDa IRE1 protein, but also the emergence under ER stress of an additional ~55 kDa band (Figure 1B and C), indicating the formation of an N-terminal, LD-containing IRE1 fragment.
evidence: Western blot data from KMS11 and OPM2 cells treated with ER stress inducers show the appearance of IRE1 cleavage fragments.

claim: Treatment with the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD blocks generation of both the LD- and CD-containing IRE1 fragments upon ER stress.
source: Treatment of KMS11 or OPM2 cells with the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD blocked generation of both the LD- and CD-containing IRE1 fragments upon ER stress (Figure 1D and E), indicating that this cleavage of IRE1 requires caspase activity.
evidence: Western blot data show that zVAD treatment prevents IRE1 cleavage in response to ER stress.

claim: The major caspase cleavage sites in IRE1 are located at aspartic acid residues 507 and 512 within the linker region.
source: Although alanine substitution of either aspartic acid 507 or 512 alone did not prevent IRE1 processing in response to ER stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), replacement of both residues blocked most of the cleavage (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Site-directed mutagenesis experiments show that double mutation of D507A and D512A prevents most IRE1 cleavage.

claim: BAX is required for caspase-mediated processing of IRE1 under ER stress.
source: We obtained two independent BAX knockout clones, which produced no BAX protein as expected; in contrast to the WT cells, these clones showed substantially less generation of cleaved (activated) caspase-3 and lacked any detectable IRE1 fragments in response to several ER stressors (Figure 1G).
evidence: Western blot data from BAX knockout KMS11 cells show no IRE1 cleavage upon ER stress.

claim: Purified caspase-3 and caspase-7 can cleave a recombinant IRE1 protein comprising the linker, kinase and RNase domains.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, purified caspase-3 and caspase-7 performed concentration-dependent cleavage of a purified recombinant protein comprising the linker, kinase and RNase domains of IRE1 (IRE1 LKR), with slightly more efficient processing by caspase-3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assay with purified caspases and recombinant IRE1 LKR protein demonstrates direct cleavage.

claim: Caspase-mediated IRE1 processing occurs in multiple myeloma, lymphoma, and leukemia cell lines.
source: We observed a similar pattern of caspase-mediated IRE1 processing in additional MM cell lines, as well as in several different types of lymphoma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Western blot data from multiple hematopoietic cell lines show IRE1 cleavage upon ER stress.

claim: ER stress induces caspase-mediated cleavage of mouse IRE1 in murine lymphoma cells and primary bone marrow-derived dendritic cells.
source: Consistent with the homology between the human and mouse orthologs, ER stress induced caspase-mediated cleavage of mouse IRE1 in two types of murine lymphoma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and F). Similar processing occurred also in mouse primary bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDC), which already exhibited some IRE1 cleavage at baseline (Figure 1H).
evidence: Western blot data from mouse cells show IRE1 cleavage similar to human cells.

claim: The LDTM fragment of IRE1 is associated primarily with the membrane compartment, whereas the CD products are found mostly in the cytosolic fraction.
source: Subcellular fractionation of OPM2 cells confirmed that the LDTM polypeptide was associated primarily with the membrane compartment, whereas the CD products were found mostly in the cytosolic fraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: Subcellular fractionation experiments show differential localization of IRE1 cleavage products.

claim: The LDTM fragment increases in abundance over 8 hr after ER stress induction, while the CD fragment accumulates over the first 4 hr and then declines.
source: In both OPM2 and KMS11 cells, the LDTM fragment increased in abundance over 8 hr after Tg addition, while the CD fragment accumulated over the first 4 hr and then declined (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Time-course western blot data show differential stability of IRE1 cleavage products.

claim: In the absence of de novo protein synthesis, caspases can cleave much of the available cellular pool of IRE1 in response to ER stress.
source: Remarkably, the amount of full-length IRE1 protein substantially decreased over this period of ER stress, while caspase inhibition by zVAD blocked the drop, preserving most of the initial full-length IRE1 protein (Figure 2B and C). Thus, in the absence of de novo protein synthesis, caspases can cleave much of the available cellular pool of IRE1 in response to ER stress.
evidence: Western blot data from cells treated with cycloheximide show extensive IRE1 cleavage that is blocked by zVAD.

claim: Caspase inhibition with zVAD stabilizes full-length IRE1 protein and augments IRE1 phosphorylation and XBP1s production under ER stress.
source: Treatment with zVAD before Tg addition indeed stabilized the full-length IRE1 protein and augmented IRE1 phosphorylation. Although XBP1s protein levels declined over time, likely due to the addition of CHX, zVAD treatment enhanced XBP1s production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the stabilization of IRE1.
evidence: Western blot data show increased IRE1 phosphorylation and XBP1s levels with zVAD treatment.

claim: Ectopic LDTM expression improves viability and diminishes caspase-3/7 activation in KMS11 cells under ER stress.
source: Surprisingly, ectopic LDTM expression improved viability and diminished caspase-3/7 activation in KMS11 cells as compared to untransfected counterparts under Tg-induced ER stress (Figure 3A and B), indicating apoptosis attenuation.
evidence: Cell viability and caspase activity assays show protective effects of LDTM expression.

claim: LDTM expression reduces caspase-3/7 activation in response to diverse ER stressors including SubAB, Tg, Tm, and BfeA.
source: Reassuringly, expression of this LDTM version also reduced caspase-3/7 activation in response to diverse ER stressors, including SubAB, Tg, Tm, and BfeA, in KMS11 or JJN3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D, F and G).
evidence: Caspase activity assays show LDTM reduces caspase activation across multiple ER stress conditions.

claim: LDTM co-localizes with the ER membrane marker Calnexin in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Consistent with this localization, immunofluorescence analysis showed co-staining of the transfected LDTM fragment with the ER membrane marker Calnexin in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy shows co-localization of LDTM with ER marker.

claim: LDTM suppresses apoptotic caspase activation independently of full-length IRE1.
source: Importantly, cells expressing ectopic LDTM showed improved viability and diminished caspase-3/7 activation under Tg- or Tm-induced ER stress, regardless of DOX treatment (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G). This data demonstrates that apoptosis attenuation by LDTM is equally effective in the presence or absence of endogenous IRE1.
evidence: Experiments with IRE1 knockdown show LDTM retains protective function without endogenous IRE1.

claim: Ectopic LDTM expression does not alter IRE1 activity in response to ER stress, as measured by XBP1s mRNA and protein levels.
source: However, consistent with its IRE1-independent function, ectopic LDTM expression did not alter IRE1 activity in response to ER stress, as measured by the levels of XBP1s mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and by mRNA levels of the known RIDD target, DGAT2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RT-qPCR and western blot data show no change in IRE1 activity markers with LDTM expression.

claim: LDTM expression does not inhibit ATF6 activation by ER stress, as gauged by levels of BiP.
source: Furthermore, LDTM expression did not inhibit ATF6 activation by ER stress, as gauged by levels of the key UPR chaperone BiP—a transcriptional target of ATF6 (Walter and Ron, 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Western blot data show BiP levels are unchanged by LDTM expression, indicating no effect on ATF6.

claim: LDTM expression does not decrease PERK activation, as judged by the levels of ATF4 and CHOP.
source: nor did it decrease PERK activation, as judged by the levels of the PERK-regulated transcription factors ATF4 and CHOP, both of which are implicated in driving apoptosis downstream to PERK (Tabas and Ron, 2011; Han et al., 2013).
evidence: Western blot data show ATF4 and CHOP levels are unchanged by LDTM expression, indicating no effect on PERK.

claim: LDTM-transfected KMS11 clones display approximately 1.5-fold higher baseline levels of BAX compared to parental controls.
source: LDTM-transfected KMS11 clones displayed approximately 1.5-fold higher baseline levels of BAX as compared to parental controls (Figure 4A), perhaps reflecting a compensatory upregulation of BAX in response to the cytoprotection provided by LDTM.
evidence: Western blot quantification shows increased BAX protein levels in LDTM-expressing cells.

claim: Ectopic LDTM expression attenuates the relative increase in mitochondrial BAX and the coordinated decrease in cytosolic BAX upon ER stress.
source: Nevertheless, ectopic LDTM expression attenuated the relative increase in mitochondrial BAX and the coordinated decrease in cytosolic BAX upon ER stress (Figure 4A).
evidence: Subcellular fractionation and western blot data show LDTM reduces BAX translocation to mitochondria.

claim: LDTM expression inhibits mitochondrial depolarization in cells undergoing ER stress in response to SubAB or Tg.
source: Consistent with its ability to decrease mitochondrial recruitment of BAX, LDTM expression also inhibited mitochondrial depolarization in cells undergoing ER stress in response to SubAB or Tg (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data using JC-1 dye show reduced mitochondrial depolarization with LDTM expression.

claim: LDTM attenuates the uptake of calcium by mitochondria during ER stress.
source: Furthermore, LDTM attenuated the uptake of calcium by mitochondria – a characteristic apoptotic event which was similarly curtailed by BAX KO (Figure 4C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data using Rhod-2 dye show reduced mitochondrial calcium uptake with LDTM expression.

claim: LDTM attenuates the Tg-induced drop in mitochondrial cytochrome C levels and the corresponding gain in cytosolic cytochrome C.
source: LDTM also attenuated the Tg-induced drop in mitochondrial cytochrome C levels and the corresponding gain in cytosolic cytochrome C (Figure 4D).
evidence: Subcellular fractionation and western blot data show LDTM reduces cytochrome C release from mitochondria.

claim: LDTM attenuates Tg-induced activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3/7.
source: Moreover, LDTM attenuated Tg-induced activation of caspase-9, known to be triggered in the cytosol through cytochrome C-induced assembly of the apoptosome, as well as the activation of caspase-3/7 downstream (Figure 4E).
evidence: Caspase activity assays show LDTM reduces activation of both caspase-9 and caspase-3/7.

claim: The BCL2 small molecule inhibitor ABT-199 reverses LDTM's attenuation of mitochondrial calcium uptake and caspase-3/7 activation in cells undergoing Tg-induced ER stress.
source: Further supporting the conclusion that LDTM regulates apoptosis via BAX, the BCL2 small molecule inhibitor ABT-199, which prevents BAX blockade by BCL2 (Ashkenazi et al., 2017), reversed LDTM's attenuation of mitochondrial calcium uptake and of caspase-3/7 activation in cells undergoing Tg-induced ER stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Flow cytometry and caspase activity assays show ABT-199 overcomes LDTM's protective effects.

claim: Ectopic LDTM expression augments proliferation of KMS11 cells restricted on matrigel.
source: Ectopic LDTM expression augmented proliferation of KMS11 cells restricted on matrigel, as measured by confluence analysis over several days using an Incucyte S3 instrument (Figure 5A).
evidence: Live-cell imaging data show increased cell growth with LDTM expression.

claim: Ectopic LDTM expression significantly enhances the growth of KMS11 tumor xenografts in vivo.
source: Importantly, ectopic LDTM expression significantly enhanced the growth of KMS11 tumor xenografts in vivo (Figure 5B).
evidence: Tumor volume measurements in mouse xenograft experiments show enhanced tumor growth with LDTM expression.

claim: IRE1 depletion by shRNA inhibits KMS11 cell growth both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Furthermore, while IRE1 depletion by shRNA inhibited KMS11 cell growth both in vitro and in vivo, in keeping with the cytoprotective role of this UPR sensor (Harnoss et al., 2019), expression of LDTM nevertheless accelerated growth even in the context of IRE1 knockdown (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Growth assays and tumor volume measurements show IRE1 knockdown reduces growth, but LDTM can still enhance growth.

claim: KMS11 tumors constitutively produce an endogenous LDTM fragment.
source: Of note, KMS11 tumors constitutively produced an endogenous LDTM fragment, suggesting that cell stress in the tumor microenvironment drives caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1.
evidence: Western blot analysis of tumor lysates shows presence of endogenous LDTM fragment.

claim: IRE1 possesses tandem cytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase and endoribonuclease (RNase) enzymatic modules, tethered to the ER membrane through an 80-amino-acid linker region.
source: IRE1 possesses tandem cytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase and endoribonuclease (RNase) enzymatic modules, tethered to the ER membrane through an 80-amino-acid linker region (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural description of IRE1 based on established knowledge.

claim: Upon sensing ER stress, IRE1 forms homodimers, which perform trans-autophosphorylation of the kinase moiety, leading to RNase engagement.
source: Upon sensing ER stress, IRE1 forms homodimers, which perform trans-autophosphorylation of the kinase moiety, leading to RNase engagement.
evidence: This describes the known mechanism of IRE1 activation based on established literature.

claim: The RNase module of IRE1 activates the transcription factor spliced X-box protein 1 (XBP1s) through non-conventional mRNA editing.
source: The RNase activates the transcription factor spliced X-box protein 1 (XBP1s) through non-conventional mRNA editing.
evidence: This describes the known function of IRE1's RNase activity based on established literature.

claim: XBP1s activates numerous genes that promote ER adaptation, ERAD, and cytoprotection.
source: In turn, XBP1s activates numerous genes that promote ER adaptation, ERAD, and cytoprotection (Acosta-Alvear et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the known function of XBP1s supported by citation.

claim: The RNase module of IRE1 helps reduce ER-associated translational load through regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD).
source: The RNase module also helps reduce ER-associated translational load through regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD) (Hollien et al., 2009)
evidence: This describes the known RIDD function of IRE1 supported by citation.

claim: RIDD can contribute to cytoprotection by regulating specific, functionally relevant genes.
source: which also can contribute to cytoprotection by regulating specific, functionally relevant genes (Lu et al., 2014; Bae et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the cytoprotective function of RIDD supported by citations.

claim: IRE1α is the most evolutionarily conserved of the UPR sensors, displaying structural and functional homology in yeast, flies, worms, fish and primates.
source: IRE1α (sometimes called ERN1) is the most evolutionarily conserved of the UPR sensors, displaying structural and functional homology in yeast, flies, worms, fish and primates.
evidence: This describes the evolutionary conservation of IRE1 based on established knowledge.

claim: PERK phosphorylates eukaryotic translation-initiation factor α (eIF2α) in response to ER stress.
source: In response to ER stress, PERK phosphorylates eukaryotic translation-initiation factor α (eIF2α) (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This describes the known function of PERK supported by citation.

claim: PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α suppresses general translation, yet induces expression of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4).
source: This suppresses general translation, yet induces expression of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4).
evidence: This describes the known downstream effects of PERK activation based on established knowledge.

claim: ATF4 stimulates genes that support ER adaptation, including one encoding the transcription factor C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP).
source: In turn, ATF4 stimulates a number of genes that support ER adaptation, including one encoding the transcription factor C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP).
evidence: This describes the known function of ATF4 based on established knowledge.

claim: The metazoan UPR triggers apoptotic cell elimination in the event that ER-stress mitigation fails.
source: However, the metazoan UPR performs an important additional function: it triggers apoptotic cell elimination in the event that ER-stress mitigation fails (Tabas and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This describes the known proapoptotic function of the UPR supported by citation.

claim: The PERK branch of the UPR plays a key role in driving apoptosis in the context of irresolvable ER stress through mechanisms that involve ATF4 and CHOP and converge on BAX.
source: The PERK branch of the UPR plays a key role in driving apoptosis in the context of irresolvable ER stress, through mechanisms that involve ATF4 and CHOP and converge on BAX (Lu et al., 2014; Tabas and Ron, 2011; Puthalakath et al., 2007; Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the known proapoptotic function of PERK supported by multiple citations.

claim: BOK is an ER-resident BCL2 family protein that is kept at low levels by ERAD but accumulates when ERAD is diverted toward unfolded proteins.
source: An additional proapoptotic signal involves the ER-resident BCL2 family protein BOK, which is kept at low levels by ERAD but accumulates when ERAD is diverted toward unfolded proteins (Llambi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the known regulation of BOK supported by citation.

claim: Physiological levels of IRE1 suppress apoptosis activation by mediating degradation of DR5 mRNA via RIDD during the early phase of the UPR.
source: In contrast to PERK, physiological levels of IRE1 suppress apoptosis activation, by mediating degradation of DR5 mRNA via RIDD during the early phase of the UPR (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the known antiapoptotic function of IRE1 supported by citation.

claim: If ER stress persists, PERK-dependent attenuation of IRE1 via the phosphatase RPAP2 inhibits RIDD, allowing DR5 levels to rise and thereby driving apoptosis.
source: If ER stress persists, PERK-dependent attenuation of IRE1 via the phosphatase RPAP2 inhibits RIDD, allowing DR5 levels to rise and thereby driving apoptosis (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the known mechanism of IRE1 regulation by PERK supported by citation.

claim: In mouse liver cells, BAX and BAK support activation of IRE1 by direct interaction with its cytoplasmic region.
source: In mouse liver cells, BAX and BAK support activation of IRE1 by direct interaction with its cytoplasmic region (Hetz et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a known interaction between BAX/BAK and IRE1 supported by citation.

claim: The ER-resident antiapoptotic protein BAX inhibitor-1 inhibits IRE1 activation through cytoplasmic association.
source: Conversely, the ER-resident antiapoptotic protein BAX inhibitor-1 inhibits IRE1 activation through cytoplasmic association (Lisbona et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes a known regulatory mechanism of IRE1 supported by citation.

claim: There is preliminary evidence that caspases may cleave PERK.
source: In addition, there is preliminary evidence that caspases may cleave PERK (Shimbo et al., 2012)
evidence: This references prior work suggesting PERK cleavage by caspases.

claim: There is preliminary evidence that caspases may cleave IRE1.
source: and IRE1 (Tang et al., 2018)
evidence: This references prior work suggesting IRE1 cleavage by caspases.

claim: Apoptosis is a built-in cell-suicide program that is shared by most metazoans.
source: Apoptosis is a built-in cell-suicide program that is shared by most metazoans (Kerr et al., 1972; Ellis and Horvitz, 1986; Hengartner and Horvitz, 1994).
evidence: This describes the fundamental nature of apoptosis supported by citations.

claim: The core intracellular apoptotic machinery entails a family of cysteine-dependent, aspartate-specific proteases, called caspases.
source: The core intracellular apoptotic machinery entails a family of cysteine-dependent, aspartate-specific proteases, called caspases (Thornberry and Lazebnik, 1998; Salvesen and Ashkenazi, 2011).
evidence: This describes the fundamental components of apoptosis supported by citations.

claim: Two interconnected signaling cascades control caspase activation in response to severe cellular stress or damage: the intrinsic (or mitochondrial) pathway and the extrinsic (or death-receptor) pathway.
source: Two interconnected signaling cascades control caspase activation in response to severe cellular stress or damage: the intrinsic (or mitochondrial) pathway and the extrinsic (or death-receptor) pathway (Martin and Green, 1995; Ashkenazi and Dixit, 1998; Danial and Korsmeyer, 2004).
evidence: This describes the known apoptotic pathways supported by citations.

claim: BAX mediates mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) through oligomerization and pore formation.
source: These signals often converge on the proapoptotic BCL2 family protein BAX (and/or its relative BAK), which mediates mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) through oligomerization and pore formation (Youle and Strasser, 2008).
evidence: This describes the known mechanism of BAX function supported by citation.

claim: MOMP releases cytochrome C from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol.
source: This releases cytochrome C from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol.
evidence: This describes a known consequence of MOMP based on established knowledge.

claim: In the cytosol, cytochrome C helps nucleate the apoptosome complex, which sets off an enzymatic cascade involving the initiator protease caspase-9 and the executioner proteases caspase-3 and caspase-7.
source: In the cytosol, cytochrome C helps nucleate the apoptosome complex, which sets off an enzymatic cascade involving the initiator protease caspase-9 and the executioner proteases caspase-3 and caspase-7 (Slee et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the known apoptosome-mediated caspase activation supported by citation.

claim: Caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1 during ER stress produces a membrane-tethered, lumenal product that feeds back onto the apoptotic signaling cascade to inhibit further caspase activation.
source: These results demonstrate that LDTM inhibits apoptotic caspase activation upon ER stress. By extension, caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1 during ER stress produces a membrane-tethered, lumenal product of IRE1 that in turn feeds back onto the apoptotic signaling cascade to inhibit further caspase activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing LDTM's antiapoptotic effects.

claim: The generation of LDTM through IRE1 cleavage provides a fail-safe checkpoint to ensure that cells with still remediable ER stress do not commit unnecessarily to apoptotic suicide.
source: A simple and plausible explanation for this apparent paradox is that the generation of LDTM through IRE1 cleavage provides a fail-safe checkpoint to ensure that cells with still remediable ER stress do not commit unnecessarily to apoptotic suicide.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Only if ER stress exceeds a cell's capacity for mitigation does sufficient caspase activity develop to override the LDTM checkpoint and fully execute apoptotic elimination.
source: Only if ER stress exceeds a cell's capacity for mitigation does sufficient caspase activity develop to override this checkpoint and fully execute apoptotic elimination.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how the LDTM checkpoint might be overcome.

claim: The cytoplasmic location of the prominent cleavage sites within IRE1 is consistent with the fact that caspase activity resides primarily in the cytosol.
source: The cytoplasmic location of the prominent cleavage sites within IRE1 is consistent with the fact that caspase activity resides primarily in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known caspase localization.

claim: The linker region of IRE1 may be more accessible to caspases than other, perhaps more buried, cytoplasmic domains.
source: Furthermore, the linker region of IRE1 may be more accessible to caspases than other, perhaps more buried, cytoplasmic domains.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why the linker region is preferentially cleaved.

claim: Presenilin-1 cleaves IRE1 within the linker region in COS7 cells.
source: Of interest, earlier work characterizing ectopically expressed IRE1 in COS7 cells showed that presenilin-1 cleaves IRE1 within the linker (Niwa et al., 1999)
evidence: This references prior work showing IRE1 cleavage by presenilin-1.

claim: IRE1 processing by apoptotic caspases occurs primarily in hematopoietic cell types, of both malignant and non-malignant origin.
source: IRE1 processing by apoptotic caspases occurred primarily in hematopoietic cell types, of both malignant and non-malignant origin.
evidence: This is a summary of the cell type specificity observed in the experimental data.

claim: Hematopoietic cells tend to express relatively high levels of IRE1 mRNA.
source: Because hematopoietic cells tend to express relatively high levels of IRE1 mRNA, it is possible that caspase-mediated processing requires abundant IRE1 protein: however, this warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the cell type specificity of IRE1 cleavage.

claim: The production of LDTM upon caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1 can significantly improve the fitness of cancer cells to survive and grow in stressful microenvironments.
source: Thus, the production of LDTM upon caspase-mediated cleavage of IRE1 can significantly improve the fitness of cancer cells to survive and grow in stressful microenvironments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro and in vivo tumor growth data.

claim: IRE1 promotes tumor growth not only in its general role as a cytoprotective UPR mediator but also in particular through its caspase-driven antiapoptotic LDTM product.
source: This conclusion has important potential implications for the role of IRE1 in hematopoietic malignancies such as MM, because it suggests that IRE1 promotes tumor growth not only in its general role as a cytoprotective UPR mediator (Harnoss et al., 2019) but also in particular through its caspase-driven antiapoptotic LDTM product.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the findings for cancer biology.

claim: Ectopic expression of the CD fragment of IRE1 (LKR) does not affect caspase-3/7 activation by Tg or SubAB.
source: In contrast to LDTM, ectopic expression of the CD fragment of IRE1 (LKR) did not affect caspase-3/7 activation by Tg or SubAB, nor did it impact LDTM's attenuation of caspase activation by these ER stressors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Caspase activity assays show LKR expression does not alter apoptotic signaling.

claim: LKR expression does not alter XBP1s levels.
source: Of note, LKR expression did not alter XBP1s levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Western blot data show no change in XBP1s with LKR expression.

claim: LDTM provides cell protection against SubAB, which induces ER stress by proteolytically cleaving BiP.
source: LDTM also provided cell protection against SubAB—which induces ER stress by proteolytically cleaving BiP (Lu et al., 2014; Paton et al., 2006) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Caspase activity assays show LDTM reduces caspase activation in response to SubAB.

claim: LDTM functions independently of the key UPR sensors IRE1, ATF6 and PERK, as well as the major ER chaperone BiP, to attenuate apoptotic caspase activation during ER stress.
source: Thus, LDTM functions independently of the key UPR sensors, IRE1, ATF6 and PERK, as well as the major ER chaperone, BiP, to attenuate apoptotic caspase activation during ER stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing LDTM does not affect UPR sensor activity.
